200	\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
201	Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
202	For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
203	Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
204	This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
205	For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.

\paragraph{Cross-configuration selection analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection} extends the selection analysis to four additional configurations.
On LLaMA SciERC, where output diversity remains substantial (18\% identical outputs, 39\% unique), LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.652) at $N{=}8$ but still falls within bootstrap noise of greedy (0.646), replicating the gap observed on Qwen SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
On CoNLL, 57--88\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples, reflecting a ceiling effect (greedy F1 ${\approx}$0.91--0.92) rather than signal failure; selection analysis on these configurations is uninformative because there is little per-sample variance for any signal to exploit.

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
VC achieves the largest gain over greedy ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions---high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence---signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap_signal_ci} reports bootstrap confidence intervals for individual signal $\rho$ and pairwise $\Delta\rho$ on SciERC NER ($N{=}8$, $n{=}529$, $B{=}10{,}000$, seed${=}42$).
The SJ--LP gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$) is clearly significant, confirming the structural advantage reported in \S\ref{sec:qe_results}.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.816$ on CoNLL); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty and task type: EM dominates easy NER (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard NER (SciERC); on RE, the hierarchy reverses---LP outperforms structural signals (3-seed; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), likely because RE's high zero-F1 rate (40\%) creates a binary-outcome regime where generation confidence is more discriminative than structural overlap.
Rankings are directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
At $N{=}16$, SJ converges to VC on NER ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); when capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significance (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the oracle headroom.
LP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, and the CDF rises smoothly with no bimodal split (Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}, Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}).
In instances with above-median LP spread ($n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.004$; $\varepsilon$ sensitivity in Table~\ref{tab:epsilon_sweep}), confirming score compression as the primary bottleneck; a free-form ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) shows this persists without constrained decoding.
The gap holds even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
Notably, LP compression's impact on quality estimation is task-dependent: despite identical compression levels, LP provides stronger QE on RE than on NER (Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), because RE's binary-outcome regime makes even compressed generation confidence more informative than structural overlap; this does not translate to selection gains on either task.

\paragraph{The gap widens with $N$.}
Doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ expands oracle headroom by $+4.4$~pp, yet LP improves by only $+0.4$~pp and VC deteriorates ($\Delta$: $-2.2{\to}{-}3.1$~pp); on RE at $N{=}16$ (preliminary), all consistency signals fall below greedy while LP is the sole positive signal ($\Delta{=}{+}0.7$~pp, $p{=}0.058$; Table~\ref{tab:re_n16_selection}).
The gap is not a small-$N$ artifact; detailed $N$-scaling analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}.

\paragraph{Ablation: free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
A natural objection is that constrained decoding artificially suppresses LP score variation by restricting the output space.
We test this with a controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$): grammar constraints are removed entirely and outputs are parsed post-hoc.
The fine-tuned model produces valid JSON at 99.95\% rate (4{,}406/4{,}408 samples), confirming format compliance without grammar enforcement.
LP score distributions are nearly identical across regimes: within-instance standard deviation ratio is $0.97{\times}$, and the tied fraction decreases by only $2$~pp (from 59.7\% to 57.7\% at $\varepsilon{=}0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}, Panel~A).
NER selection gains remain negligible under both regimes (Panel~B), confirming that LP compression is intrinsic to the model's probability assignments rather than an artifact of constrained decoding.
This rules out constrained decoding as the primary cause of the correlation-selection gap.

Our consensus-proximity selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, freitag2022high}; all variants fail because utility functions correlate with F1 across instances but not within them (Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
Per-signal quality estimation changes and an RE-specific selection interaction under free-form decoding are detailed in Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.
Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\ $0.379$ in-domain; Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
